sections.heading: The harvest of August

pairs.en: Orthodox listener! In the month of August, at the very hour of harvest, when out in the fields the ears of grain cut from the stalk are being bound into sheaves, carted into barns, and stacked into ricks — the Master of Heaven too has gathered from his field his choicest spiritual wheat, and today, with rejoicing, he sends it up to the granaries on high.

The estate is the world, as the Gospel says. The field or the cornland is this present age — or take it to mean our passing life in this world. The wheat is the righteous; the ears of grain are their good deeds, their merits. The harvest is the end of life. The sickle is the debt of death our nature owes. The steward and master of it all is God, and God has no shortage of estates. He calls himself a workman: *“My Father is working until now,”* says Christ, *“and I am working.”* [John 5:17]

sections.heading: The Virgin is God's own field

pairs.en: His own cornland is the Most Pure and Most Blessed Virgin, of whom the Church says: “You brought forth the divine Ear of Grain, as a field unploughed.” [Akathist, ikos 3] Clearly that Field, over the sixty years of her earthly life, brought forth choice ears of wheat worthy of the heavenly barns. So the good Master, God, appoints a whole day for the harvest — this fifteenth of August — and sends workmen out to his harvest: the angelic choirs. For the angels are the reapers, and they gather in the choicest earthly wheat of the whole crop — the Most Pure and Most Blessed Virgin Theotokos. On earth they gather her merits and escort them to the barns above the heavens; and they gather and escort them all together, in full assembly, for her Dormition is glorified by Powers and Thrones, Principalities and Dominions, Virtues, Cherubim and Seraphim.

The poor widow of Bethlehem, Ruth, on hearing that the good man Boaz was directing the harvest, said to her mother-in-law Naomi: *“I will go to the field and glean ears of grain behind the reapers.”* [Ruth 2:2] On the day of the Dormition of the Most Pure and Most Blessed Virgin Mary — as if at Boaz's rich harvest — heaven and earth, the Church triumphant and the Church militant, are gathering in the spiritual wheat. Heaven gathers the Theotokos's merits; earth gathers her benefactions. The Church triumphant gathers celebrations in her honour, the Church militant gathers praises. And we — what shall we do? Let us take poor Ruth for our model: let us go to the field and glean “ears of grain behind the reapers.” The field, as we already know, is the sixty-year life of the Most Pure Theotokos. That field has its furrows, its portions, in which its good ears of grain grow — deeds more pleasing to God than the ascetic feats of all the saints.

sections.heading: Five furrows, five letters of her name

pairs.en: Let us go, then, to that field with our mind, even if we follow behind everyone else, and let us gather what is left after the harvest — the remaining ears of her lofty dignities, which consist in deeds pleasing to God. Let us bind them into a single sheaf — I with my poor-witted discourse, and your piety by listening with love — and in this way let us build up a rick of the Church's praises. Yet my blunt sickle and the unskilled hand of my speech dare not reach out to the whole most holy life of the Theotokos, whom even the angelic eye cannot bear to look upon: “Hard to gaze upon even for the eyes of angels.” It dares not reach out to the loftiest and innumerable virtues of her whole harvest-field, but ventures only upon five furrows, rich enough — as we read in the Akathist, “Rejoice, furrow that makes the abundance of mercies grow” — and upon the five ears of grain growing there, which make up the five letters in the most blessed name of Mary [Мариа].

sections.heading: First furrow: the Wise Virgin (M)

pairs.en: To begin, let us step onto the first furrow, or portion, of her most holy life — the one that starts from the house of her holy and righteous parents Joachim and Anna and runs through Solomon's temple. The name of this furrow is betrothal. This furrow bore a worthy ear of grain over the course of twelve years: in a place closed to the people, in the temple, behind the inner veil, it raised the young Maiden, the Most Pure Virgin Mary, chosen before the ages to be Mother to God. Together with St Andrew of Crete we shall give the ear of this furrow a most worthy name, one that begins with the letter M, the first letter of Mary's name: “the Wise Virgin.”

That is how St Andrew magnifies her in his encomium: “the Wise Virgin.” And yet, holy Andrew, would you not do better to set her on the very highest step of wisdom, calling her the Most Wise and All-Wise Virgin — one who surpasses all, whose wisdom the Church herself acknowledges in these words: “Rejoice, receptacle of the Wisdom of God! Rejoice, you who surpass the understanding of the wise!” Come forward here, then, you wise virgins of the Gospel, and pay fitting honour to this Wisest of Virgins as your Lady! But you too, you other five, the foolish, stay here as well, so that you may learn wisdom. For this wise Virgin, filled full of the wisdom of God — being both the ear of the Bread of Life and the vine of the ripened cluster (“O Theotokos, you are the true vine that grew for us the Fruit of Life”) — at the close of her harvest-time prepares a special table for the foolish as well: *“She has prepared her table, summoning with a loud proclamation: whoever is foolish, let him turn in to me; and to those who lack understanding she said: Come, eat my bread and drink the wine I have mixed for you; leave folly behind.”* [Proverbs 9:2–6] It is as if she were saying: “Feed on the bread from the ear of grain, drink the drink from the vine, and you will leave your foolishness behind; you will be filled with understanding, with wisdom.”

sections.heading: The table she sets for the foolish

pairs.en: A marvellous table this is — extraordinary, the very opposite of our own customs! With us, when someone eats to satiety or beyond, or gets drunk on wine, he loses whatever remains of his reason, and a wise man turns into a fool. One elder in the Paterikon rightly said of himself that he knew the whole Bible by heart, with its commentary, but when he had eaten his fill of bread, he forgot it all, as if he had never read a thing. As for wine, the Apostle too advises us not to get drunk on it, telling us there is something in it that drives a man out of his mind.

Clearly, the bread and wine of the Wise Virgin are not so harmful, and have no such noxious properties. Whomever she feeds or gives to drink, she does not add to his foolishness but teaches him understanding and wisdom, for the power of that food and drink lies in its begetting of pure, virginal blood, as the prophet Zechariah foretold when he said: *“What adorns her is only the wheat of the chosen, and wine that begets virgins.”* [Zechariah 9:17] Those words deserve our attention: “wine that begets virgins.” Elsewhere wine begets impurity, but here from wine comes purity itself — virginity: “wine that begets virgins” — and the virgins here, of course, are not foolish but wise.

As the mother is, so are the daughters: this wine has a wise mother, so the wine is wise too, and the food is wise. Therefore whoever is foolish, let him turn aside to her; let him eat her bread and drink her wine, and surely one day the fool will grow wise. And you the wise, and you the foolish alike — let us walk all around this spiritual ear of grain, embrace it with devout feelings, fix upon it the eyes of our mind, draw profit from it for ourselves, and learn wisdom!

sections.heading: Joseph's granaries and our schooling

pairs.en: When Joseph of the Old Testament faithfully interpreted for Pharaoh the dream about the ears of grain he had seen, and took great care over gathering in the wheat and filling the granaries with it, Pharaoh made him ruler of all Egypt, and made his own nobles and princes Joseph's pupils: *“That he might instruct his princes as himself, and make his elders wise.”* [Psalm 104:22] And we too, O spiritual Wheat, our Nourisher — when we see the Church's granaries being filled spiritually with your lofty virtues, like choice ears for the heavenly barn, and with your benefactions, like the wheat itself — we give ourselves over to you for schooling, O Wise Virgin! We want to be your pupils: instruct us, make us wise, as Joseph did the princes and elders of Egypt!

sections.heading: She teaches by example: holy places and holy company

pairs.en: The Wise Virgin teaches not by words but by deed — by herself, by her own example. And what is it? Let us look: in what place, on what furrow, was that virtuous ear of her virginity grown? In the temple, in the sanctuary, in a place so holy it is called the Holy of Holies, where only holy people entered. Learn, then, and let everyone know: for progress in good works, a holy place and the company of devout people are a great help.

And what benefit does the company of devout people bring? It sets a person on the path of virtue. Lot is the proof of it. His virtue is a thing to marvel at: living in Sodom among the most lawless of men, he did not lose his virtue, his fear of God. Where did so mighty a piety take shape in him, that those dreadful iniquities did it no harm at all? The example shows where it came from: he was brought up at the side of a righteous man — Abraham — and thanks to him perfected himself in virtue. This interpretation belongs to St Chrysostom, who puts it this way: “What raised righteous Lot to the height of such great virtue was the friendship he had with the patriarch Abraham, and it worked so powerfully in him that even in Sodom he followed in Abraham's footsteps.” All the lawless abominations of that city could not corrupt Lot's virtues, because from his earliest years he had been steeped in virtue thanks to righteous Abraham. Such is the company of the devout!

sections.heading: What she grew into

pairs.en: The Most Pure and Most Blessed Virgin Mary spent the time of her youth in a holy place; she never left the temple of the Lord, living among devout people, among the high priests. And into what strength did she grow through this? Look: she made the streams of the river run backwards; she dried up, as it were, a flood, as Moses did the sea — the flood of original sin, which was seizing the souls of the innocent: *“Death reigned even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of Adam's transgression.”* [Romans 5:14] That flood she crossed dry-shod, conceiving and bearing without stain, and in this way she led the human race up from the very bottom of that abyss onto dry ground: *“Our soul has passed through the rushing water.”* [Psalm 123:4–5] And our soul passed through under the guidance of a wise Leader — the Most Pure Virgin — which is why “your people keep festival, delivered from the guilt of sin.”

She stopped the sun more majestically than Joshua the son of Nun: he stopped the material sun, she the spiritual Sun of Righteousness — God; he over Gibeon, she in her most pure virginal womb; he for a few hours, until the people of Israel had avenged themselves on their enemies, but she for nine months. What am I saying — nine months? For thirty-three years, until the head of the enemy, the devil, was utterly crushed!

Righteous Lot, too, she surpassed in her holiness. He kept himself in one dishonourable city, but the Most Pure Virgin, in the whole world that lies in evil, took no harm to her immaculate life. The whole world is like a thorn-brake — she alone in it is the rose, the lily among thorns. The whole world is like a swamp — she alone in it is gold. The whole world is like a sea flooded with bitter, brackish waters — she alone in it is like a river of sweet waters, untouched by the bitterness.

sections.heading: The river that flows through the sea

pairs.en: Well-informed people report that somewhere in the world there is a certain river which flows right across the sea, and yet mingles none of its sweet waters with the bitter waters of the sea — evidently this happens by a special miracle of God. And the sea cannot break that river or mix its waters with its own. St Gregory Nazianzen recalls this in his verses, in which he lays down laws for those who keep virginity; and the verses read like this: “There is found a river flowing through the sea, whose sweet waters mingle not with the bitter; and then one may draw sweet water out of the sea. But will the shipmasters ever chance upon that river?” So says St Gregory Nazianzen.

The life of each of us in this world is like a river: *“I was poured out like water,”* says David; and the sweet river is the holy cross that is laid upon us. When we empty ourselves into the sea of worldly passions, we lose our sweetness.

Great are you, Dnieper, and you give drink to many; but draw near the sea, and no one will want to know you any longer, or lift your waters to his lips: you become unpalatable, salty, bitter, having mixed yourself with the salty, bitter waters of the sea.

Great rivers are you also, you who make efforts and strive to serve God. Of you it was said in heaven to the Theologian in Revelation: *“The waters that you saw are peoples and nations.”* [Revelation 17:15] But then it is dreadful even to look at you as soon as you touch the sea of this passionate world: nothing will remain of you, and you will turn bitter: *“He who touches pitch will be blackened by it, and he who keeps company with the perverse will be corrupted.”* [Sirach 13:1; Proverbs 13:21]

Happy the river that flows through the sea and yet does not mingle itself with the sea! Happy the servant of God who lives in the midst of the world and yet has no communion with the world, like Lot in the midst of the lawless! Just such a spiritual stream, such a river, was the Wise Virgin, the Most Pure and Most Blessed Mary. She ran the whole course of her life through the sea of this world — and did she take on even the least share of sinful worldly passion? Not in the least! The Holy Spirit tastes those sweet waters of her sinless life and, as if savouring the finest of drinks, says in the Song of Songs: *“You are all fair, my Beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”* [Song of Songs 4:1]

sections.heading: Purity of body and purity of spirit

pairs.en: With dry feet the son of Nun crosses the streams of the Jordan. With righteousness unimpaired Lot walks in the midst of Sodom. Just as blamelessly does the Most Holy Virgin pass her life, dwelling in the body in the world, in the midst of a stubborn and corrupt generation. And the beginning of it all was the temple of the Lord and the company of the righteous. Now she enters the promised land with joy, and — being the Wise Virgin — by her example she teaches us to care constantly for the holy places of the Lord's churches and for the company of the righteous. And whoever drops and sows the hours of his life on furrows like these will without doubt grow into a rich ear of grain and, as Christ's wheat, will be gathered into the granary on high. By her example the Wise Virgin also teaches purity — and a twofold purity: outward and inward, of body and of soul. Of her the Holy Spirit says in the Song of Songs: *“Your belly is like a heap of wheat set about with lilies.”* [Song of Songs 7:3]

The heap of wheat signifies Christ, born of her, who said: *“I am the Bread.”* [John 6:35] Like a grain of wheat fallen into the earth he died, yet he serves as abundant nourishment for all, like a heap of wheat and more, for he satisfies everyone abundantly: *“You open your hand and fill every living thing with your good pleasure”* [Psalm 144:16]; *“when you open your hand, all will be filled with good.”* [Psalm 103:28]

The lilies here signify the immaculate virginity of the Most Holy Virgin. It is worth pausing to ask why the Holy Spirit, in describing virginal fruitfulness, speaks of only one heap of a single kind of wheat, yet expresses the virginity in a multitude of lilies. She has one heap of wheat, because once and once only she bore the one Christ; but the lilies of her purity are many. St Epiphanius says of her: “She was a Virgin not only in body but also in spirit.” Blamelessness of body is one lily; purity of spirit is another lily; and Christ is in the middle, between the outward and the inward virginity of his Most Pure Mother, the bodily and the spiritual, like a heap of wheat among the lilies.

Where there is only one lily — where the body alone is kept pure while the spirit gives itself over to sins — do not look there for the wheat of Christ; not merely no heap of it, but not even a single grain of his grace. This is exactly what one of the teachers points out: “Scripture does not say: a heap within a lily, but among the lilies — in view of the two lilies of virginity: one which is within, in the intentions of the spirit, and the other which is outside, in the body, and signifies incorruption.” The outward lily without the inward lily is nothing, for without the resolve of the spirit the incorruption of the body is vain.

sections.heading: Second furrow: the Ewe-Lamb of Christ (A)

pairs.en: Having thus learned understanding from the Wise Virgin, we take from the first furrow, the first portion of her life, her ear of grain, and we hold it in the hand of our unforgetting memory until we have gathered the other ears and made of them a whole sheaf. From the first furrow of the Theotokos's most holy life let us step across to the next, which lies under Joseph's roof, in the house of Joseph. It begins from Solomon's temple, and it ends in the cave of Bethlehem, by the field of Salome, a woman of Bethlehem. This furrow, which bore an ear worthy of Mary's lofty virtue, takes its name from the second letter of her most blessed name — A: “the Ewe-Lamb of Christ” [Agnitsa]. So she is magnified by St Germanus and St George of Nicomedia in their discourses, and above all by St John Damascene in his fortieth discourse on her Nativity, where he says: “You are the Ewe-Lamb, from whom the Shepherd clothed himself in the sheep, and you tear apart and put to death the old garments.” And in the Akathist we read: “Rejoice, Ewe-Lamb, who bore the Lamb of God.”

And yet, Most Pure Virgin! You deserve to be named not after the dumb beasts, but after creatures endowed with speech and reason. You deserve that all the Church's teachers, gathered together, should magnify you as a single Angel higher than all other Angels, as Queen of all the Angels — more honourable than the Cherubim, more glorious than the Seraphim. Truly you deserve it; and yet when they magnify her as the Ewe-Lamb, by that very name they best display her dignity and explain her royal crown, her pre-eminence over the Angels. The moment the lips pronounce these words — “the Ewe-Lamb who bore the Lamb” — there comes at once to mind the might and power and glory and kingdom of the Lamb, of which the holy Theologian says: *“Every creature that is in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, I heard saying: To him who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb, be blessing and honour and glory and dominion for ever and ever.”* [Revelation 5:13]

sections.heading: The power of the Lamb is sinlessness

pairs.en: They say the lion is king over all the beasts, and that mighty bears and fierce leopards tremble before his strength. But the Lamb who sits on the throne reigns not only over the beasts but over all creatures in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Angels and men bow down to him, and every creature obeys him.

Where then does the Lamb get such strength? Where does his almighty authority come from? Let us put the question to St Irenaeus, who discusses this very point and says: “No one else could open the book of the Father and look upon it, except the Lamb that was slain, because *he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.”* [1 Peter 2:22] From this we also know that what raised the Lamb to so high a royal dignity was precisely that “he committed no sin.” His very guilelessness makes him King, and every creature in heaven or on earth spreads itself out at his feet in lowest prostration, because “he committed no sin.”

When the Holy Fathers named above magnify the Most Pure and Most Blessed Virgin as the Ewe-Lamb, all creation declares its allegiance to her. Heaven prepares for her a royal crown of stars, a radiant purple robe of the sun, a beautiful footstool of the moon. And you, Cherubim, be her throne; and you, Seraphim, serve her as slaves serve a monarch. All you Angels, give her the bow that is her due, as your Queen; and let all creation come, fall down, and worship her, saying: “Blessing, honour and glory to the Most Pure and Most Blessed Virgin Mary, for she is the Ewe-Lamb, for she is guileless, for she committed no sin, and no deceit was in her mouth.” Her very lamb-likeness makes her the all-powerful Lady; her very guilelessness crowns her with a kingdom; and to call her the Ewe-Lamb means the same as to call her Queen of the Angels. Through guilelessness the crown of the eternal kingdom is hallowed.

sections.heading: The Lamb draws down God

pairs.en: This Immaculate Ewe-Lamb, led from Solomon's temple into the house of a righteous man, St Joseph, drew upon herself the eyes of God the Father, who says: *“To whom will I look, but to the meek and humble, who trembles at my words.”* [Isaiah 66:2] She won the heart of God the Son, who says: *“You have captured us, our Sister, our Bride; you have captured us with one glance of your eyes”* [Song of Songs 4:9] — that is, by your purity, in which, as in a clear eye, there is not so much as a speck of dust. That bright eye is a pure conscience, on which God gazes, for *“man looks on the face, but God looks on the heart”* [1 Kingdoms 16:7] — on the conscience. This Guileless Ewe-Lamb also drew near to God the Holy Spirit, who says: *“The guileless and the upright have joined themselves to me; and he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with the Lord.”* [Psalm 24:21; 1 Corinthians 6:17]

Thus, giving herself over to God in Trinity by her lamb-like guilelessness, she draws the inhabitants of heaven down to herself. The Archangel Gabriel flies swiftly down, and soon the bodiless one stood beneath Joseph's roof. After him comes God the Word with the Holy Spirit, while God the Father looks on with favour, gazing graciously upon it from the height of his glory: *“For God so loved the world that he gave his Only-begotten Son.”* [John 3:16] Heaven rejoices, earth marvels: “The things of heaven were glad with love, and the things of earth were seized with trembling awe, when the most holy voice came upon you, O Theotokos!” O power of lamb-like guilelessness and virginal dignity — what are you not counted worthy of through your innocence, through your guilelessness?

Then, arriving at the appointed time at the place named “the house of bread” — that is, Bethlehem — she becomes a single ear of grain full of life: she brings Christ into the world as an ear of grain brings forth the wheat kernel, and for the Lamb born of her she becomes a pasture of wheat: “They behold him as a blameless Lamb, pastured in the womb of Mary.”

We kiss you with heartfelt love, O good Ear of grain, ensouled with the guilelessness of the Lamb! And that good consecration of yours at Bethlehem we sow and root deep in our hearts like a seed of wheat — if only we could root there even the very least little particle of your guilelessness, and make it our inheritance!

sections.heading: Third furrow: the Handmaid of the Lord (R)

pairs.en: From Bethlehem begins the third furrow of the Theotokos's most holy life. It runs through Egypt, turns back from Egypt towards Nazareth, and reaches even to the places near the hill of Golgotha. This furrow grew for us no small ear of grain, one beginning with the third letter of her most blessed name — R: “the Handmaid of the Lord” [Raba]. So she named herself even earlier, at the hour of the Annunciation, when she said to the Angel: *“Behold the Handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.”* [Luke 1:38] From her childhood, brought into the temple at three years of age, she was already serving God with diligence; but she began to serve him still more, in a special way, when after his incorrupt birth she wrapped him in swaddling clothes, nursed him at Nazareth in the days of his boyhood, and cared for his honourable upbringing until he came to manhood. After the death of St Joseph she earned food and clothing for herself and for him by the labour of her own hands, and at that time she was in the fullest sense the Handmaid of the Lord, rendering, besides her spiritual labour, the bodily services of a servant, with a mother's love.

sections.heading: Serving as the cherubim serve

pairs.en: “The Handmaid of the Lord.” Service of the Lord is a special kind of service, and more than once in Holy Scripture it is expressed through the Cherubim. The prophet Ezekiel saw the house of God surrounded by Cherubim: *“And the Cherubim stood on the right side of the house; the glory of the Lord went out from the threshold of the house and rested above the Cherubim, and the Cherubim lifted up their wings.”* [Ezekiel 10:2, 18–19] And when God commanded Moses to build him the Tabernacle of meeting, he ordered that whole temple to be adorned with Cherubim: *“Let there be figures of Cherubim everywhere.”* [see Exodus 26:1] In the Tabernacle of meeting, as later in Solomon's temple, besides the two Cherubim above the Ark of the covenant, wherever you looked — on the walls, on the doors, on the pillars, on the veils and the windows — you could see the image of Cherubim; and this was a sign of the presence of God, with the Cherubim standing before him in servile attendance. And although with the Lord God all the Angels are servants, ministering to him and standing before him — *“Are they not all ministering spirits?”* [Hebrews 1:14] — nevertheless the Cherubim serve in a special way: while the others are sent out on service, as it is written, *“sent forth to minister”* [ibid.], the Cherubim remain in attendance without ever departing.

Angels, go and guard mankind! Archangels, go and bear good tidings! Dominions, go and govern the kingdoms of the nations; Virtues, go to war; Powers, go work wonders; you other choirs, carry out the duties laid upon you. But you Cherubim — stand at the resting-place of God (“the Cherubim stood on the right side of the house” — Ezekiel 10:3) and attend upon his majesty. Bear him up without ceasing: *“He who sits upon the Cherubim; he mounted upon the Cherubim and flew; he sped upon the wings of the wind”* [Psalm 17:11; 79:2] — and this you do properly in the temple of the Lord, where the glory of the Lord is present: *“The house of the Lord was filled with glory.”* [2 Chronicles 5:14]

By many examples it has been made plain that God is surrounded on every side by cherubic service, and whoever wants to serve him well must serve as a Cherub serves. So the Church remembers the three youths who served God in the Babylonian furnace: “Made like the Cherubim, the youths in the furnace.”

sections.heading: Foolish service, hired service, cherubic service

pairs.en: How then does one serve God in the cherubic way? “Cherub,” according to Augustine, translates from the Hebrew as “fullness of understanding”; consequently, whoever wants to serve God in the cherubic way must serve him with understanding, wisely, and not foolishly. For there are some — and I may well be among them — who serve God not with understanding but rather foolishly. A man serves, he labours, labours even strenuously; yet he does it all not properly for God, but rather for the sake of vain praise from men, in order to be well known among men. Or if he does hide from human sight, still within himself, in his own mind, he grows vainglorious and thinks himself a saint. *“He who considers himself to be something, being nothing, deceives himself.”* [Galatians 6:3] Such a man serves God foolishly, unwisely — not in the cherubic way.

There are others who serve God not indeed for vainglory or any self-conceit, but nevertheless for their own private profit and advantage — so that a reward may be given them in heaven — and not properly for God. This service too is not cherubic but merely human; not according to the cherubic fullness of understanding, but according to human self-love: such a man wishes good above all to himself, loves himself more than God. Such service is, properly speaking, the service of a hireling, just as a hireling serves his master so that the master will pay him.

But the cherubic service of the Lord is done according to fullness of understanding — intelligently, wisely; not for any private gain of one's own, not for vain earthly praise, not for the reward of heaven: *“What have I in heaven?* *And apart from you, what have I desired on earth?”* [Psalm 72:25] It is done properly for God alone, for the sake of his divine love. This special service according to fullness of understanding, in the cherubic way, is what pleases God most of all. Such service raises the servant to the rank of a son. It confers on such a person the dignity of sonship, just as the Angels who serve the Lord according to fullness of understanding are named sons of God, as it is written: *“The sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord.”* [Job 1:6] So too the man who serves God in the cherubic way — wisely, out of divine love and not for his own sake — becomes a son of God, for he loves God as a Father.

sections.heading: How the Handmaid served

pairs.en: But let us turn to the true Handmaid of the Lord, the Most Pure Virgin Mary, who says of herself: “Behold the Handmaid of the Lord!” How did she serve her Lord? You most wise Cherubim, yield the senior place at the Throne of God to the most wise Servant of God — the Most Holy Virgin, who served him not only in the cherubic way but above it, with her own special service according to fullness of understanding, loving him *“with all her soul, with all her heart and with all her mind.”* [Matthew 22:37] She loved with all her soul, understandingly; with all her heart, sweetly; with all her mind, unceasingly — and this for the sake of his divine love, not for any self-love or private advantage of her own.

Closest of all to the Throne of God stand the Cherubim with their servile attendance; but closer than them all is the Most Holy Virgin, of whom the Damascene says: “She is wholly the Bridal Chamber of the Spirit, wholly near to God.” Between God and the Cherubim lies the distance of the divine glory. But between God, made flesh in a virginal womb, and the Most Pure Virgin — what distance could there be? The whole of God is in her, and she is wholly in God: “Wholly the Bridal Chamber of God, wholly near to God.” The Cherubim stand before God without departing — but when is the Most Pure Virgin ever without God? God is with her and she with God in the very closest union of love. She has cleaved to him spiritually, by the very nature of motherhood, so that neither can God ever be parted from her, nor she from God: she is for ever inseparable from him, never departing.

Are the Cherubim a throne for God? Do they bear God upon themselves? Here is the “cherubic Throne — the Virgin” [heirmos of the Nativity canon]: God is carried on her bosom, on her most pure arms, in Bethlehem, Jerusalem and Egypt, as on cherubic wings. “The cherubic Throne — the Virgin.” And all her service to Christ God, born of her, even until he reached manhood, was cherubic in its fullness of understanding and wisdom, for that service was filled full of ineffable love and of a mother's love besides. And for the sake of this service of the Lord she grew into the Daughter of God the Father, as the Nomenclator says of her: “First-born Daughter of God, most dearly beloved Daughter of the Pre-eternal Father.” So high did the ear of the Handmaid's service grow, in her care to nourish the divine Child Christ, that she became the Daughter of God. If we too learned to serve God in the cherubic way, with understanding, we should truly become beloved children of God.

sections.heading: Fourth furrow: the Fountain of Life (I)

pairs.en: The fourth furrow of the Theotokos's most holy life is on Golgotha, beneath the Cross; and it brought forth an ear of grain of high dignity, one beginning with the fourth letter of Mary's most blessed name — I: “the Fountain of Life” [Istochnik]. So we read in the Menaion for January: “Rejoice, gold-streaming Fountain of immortality, pouring forth true sweetness.” The Fountain of life upon the Cross is Christ; the fountain beneath the Cross is Mary. He is pierced by nails and a spear; she by the sword foretold by the God-receiver: *“A sword shall pierce through your own soul also.”* [Luke 2:35] From the fountain of Christ flow streams of Blood; from the fountain of the Mother, streams of tears. And these two most holy fountains washed clean the swamp of our sins: the one with Blood, the other with tears. The Fountain that is Christ, by the outpouring of his Blood, was offering sacrifice to God the Father on our behalf: *“Christ died for us”* [Romans 5:8]; the fountain that is Mary, in the outpouring of her tears, stood right there with a spiritual sacrifice: *“A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit.”* [Psalm 50:19]

And God the Father, looking down from above upon the sacrifice of his Son, looked also upon the sacrifice of his Daughter; and by both those Sacrifices he was entreated and propitiated, that he might be merciful to us sinners. *“Your harvest shall come like a fountain.”* [Proverbs 6:11] Truly those words were fulfilled on Golgotha. There took place there a single harvest of our sins: he who takes upon himself the sin of the world reaped the thorny field of our iniquities and, binding them into sheaves, took them on his shoulders and lifted them up on his own Body onto the tree.

This was the harvest of all Christ's labours, undertaken on earth for our salvation. At Christ's death on the Cross they were gathered together, so as to present them all, with his sufferings, to God the Father. At this fruitful harvest the Most Pure Virgin — by her presence at that terrible struggle giving some consolation to the Workman who was dying for our salvation — showed herself, as it were, the fountain of the harvest.

sections.heading: The fountain of light on Golgotha

pairs.en: St Gregory of Neocaesarea called the Most Holy Virgin a fountain of light. There was need of light on Golgotha, when “Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, knew his own setting in death” and thick darkness covered the whole world: *“There was darkness over all the earth.”* [Matthew 27:45] Mary became a fountain of light beneath the Cross so that, like a light-bearing candle, she might shed light in place of the sun that had set, the luminary of the world. That the light might not perish when God died, she sustained it by her own radiance.
O Theotokos, our Light! Illumine our darkness! O Fountain of life! Bring to life the deadness of our souls!

sections.heading: Fifth furrow: the Crown of the Apostles (A)

pairs.en: The fifth and last furrow of the Theotokos's most holy life stretches from the hill of Golgotha and runs towards the Mount of Olives, as far as Gethsemane, for *“from that hour the disciple took her to his own home.”* [John 19:27] This furrow grew a most honoured ear of grain, held in special reverence among the saints then still living in the first Church. From the present Akathist of the Dormition we shall give that ear a name beginning with the fifth and last letter of the most blessed name “Maria” — A: “Crown of the Apostles” [Apostolam venets]. So we read in the first ikos: “Rejoice, most honoured crown of the apostles.” For at the close of the gathering of the ears it is also necessary, according to custom, to hold the harvest-home — to weave a wreath out of those same ears.

After the voluntary passion and death of their Lord, the holy apostles, as we know, were in a state of dejection, so that they had to cry out with the weeping prophet: *“The joy of our hearts has ceased; our dance has turned into mourning; the crown has fallen from our head.”* [Lamentations 5:15–16] Yet in their sorrow they had a comfort too, for their Mother the Theotokos, the Most Pure Virgin, the Joy of the sorrowing, was still alive among them.

After the Lord's Ascension the apostles again had no little sorrow and affliction. Christ's words came true: *“In the world you will have tribulation; you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice.”* [John 16:20, 33] Amid all these sorrows and griefs the holy apostles had one consolation and comfort — the bodily presence of the Most Pure and Most Blessed Virgin. By the testimony of many, whoever among the deeply sorrowful so much as looked upon her was at once filled with spiritual gladness. For from her there went out a certain special grace, comforting the weeping and gladdening the sorrowful. And in those days the Most Holy Virgin was, in the first Church, a crown of joy.

The holy apostles gather in the upper room on Sion, and in their midst, in the highest place, sits the Most Holy Virgin, like a crown. Do they offer prayers — the Most Holy Virgin is in their midst, like a crown. Do they cast lots for the preaching, do they ordain deacons, do they establish the common life — the Most Holy Virgin is among them, like a crown; and a crown of joy, consoling them in their sorrows.

sections.heading: Her care for the first Church

pairs.en: The murderers seized the holy protomartyr Stephen, led him out to the brook Kedron, into the valley of Jehoshaphat that lies between the Mount of Olives and Jerusalem, and laid their murderous hands upon him; and the Most Holy Virgin, standing at a distance on a hill with St John the Theologian and watching his death, sent up diligent prayers for him to her Son and God — and brought it about that Christ himself appeared to holy Stephen, as he was being stoned and dying, standing in the opened heaven.

King Herod raised his hands to oppress some of the first Church and killed James, the brother of John, with the sword; and the Most Pure Virgin herself commits his martyred body to burial, accompanies it to the grave, and by her prayers raises his holy soul to heaven and sets it before the Throne of God.

Holy Peter is thrown into prison, with a strong guard set over him — four squads of four soldiers; and the Most Pure Virgin, in the house of a woman who bore her own name — Mary, the mother of John — calls together the first Church and makes prayer for him, for *“the Church was praying earnestly to God for him.”* [Acts 12:5] And she obtained this: that an Angel of the Lord was sent to lead Peter out of the prison.

Oh, how much her bodily presence helped the holy apostles! Oh, how happy was the first Church, to have in its sorrows such a comfort, such help in its labours, such consolation in its griefs! She was in the midst of the assembly of the apostles like a kind of crown — like the one wreath of honour for their struggles and sufferings!

Rejoice, most honoured crown of the apostles, grown into such glory and honour among the holy apostles, like an ear of grain amid the choice wheat of the Theotokos's virtue! Already you have drawn near to your happy harvest-time; for the harvest-field is the end of life, the sickle is the debt of death our nature owes, the ears of virtue are the merits, and the reapers are the Angels.

sections.heading: The reapers are angels

pairs.en: We have now walked — though with the lazy steps of a poor-witted mind — through the field of the life of the Most Pure Virgin Theotokos; we have looked closely at her five ears of grain, worthy of their lofty names, and with our plain, common speech we have bound them, as it were, into a single sheaf — but a clumsy, unskilful one: *“Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner.”* [Sirach 15:9] Let us give way to more skilful, more practised reapers, the holy Angels, for “the reapers are the Angels.”

Fifteen years after the Lord's Ascension from earth to heaven, a council was held in heaven within the Holy Trinity: to convey the Mother of God out of the world into the dwellings beyond the world. At that very hour the Most Pure Virgin was offering her customary prayers on the Mount of Olives. And behold, a herald is sent out from the Throne of God with a branch of paradise — the same Archangel Gabriel who once brought the good tidings of God's descent from heaven to earth is sent out now to announce to the Most Pure Mother of God her glorious ascent from earth to heaven.

Does one Angel alone carry out this commission? Not one alone: now as before, a multitude of the heavenly host was with the Angel. Some of them catch the apostles up through the air and carry them, like sheaves from far-off fields, from distant lands to the little house of the Theotokos, like ricks brought to the threshing-floor; while other Angels keep watch over the books of life of the Theotokos's most holy life, and bring together into one place her great virtues, lofty dignities and merits — already well known to the Throne of God and long since recorded in heaven — for her greater honour and praise, reaping them like ears of grain from the furrows and binding them into sheaves. For it is beyond doubt true that at the death of every person all his deeds rise up, and as a man has sown, so shall he reap.

Good was the sowing, though at times hard: “They went forth and wept, casting their seeds”; but how happy, how joyful was the time of harvest — *“but those who come will come with joy, gathering their sheaves.”* [Psalm 125:6] *“Those who sow with tears will reap with joy.”* [Psalm 125:5] To all the furrows of the Theotokos's life we have mentioned, Angels came out from every side in great numbers for the common labour, to gather in the ears of her virtues.

sections.heading: The angels gather her sheaf

pairs.en: From the first furrow, where the ear is named “the Wise Virgin,” the Angels gather her ears of new vows of virginity, offered for the first time — for among womankind she was the first Virgin to bring God a vow for ever. From the next furrow of her life, where the ear is named “the Ewe-Lamb of Christ,” they gather these ears: the Powers gather her lamb-like guilelessness, for to the guileless, as was said, high authority is given; the Virtues gather her lamb-like meekness; and the Dominions her lamb-like humility, for the sake of which she is counted worthy of dominion over all the world: *“He who humbles himself will be exalted.”* [Matthew 23:12] From the third furrow, where the ear is “the Handmaid of the Lord,” the Cherubim gather the ears of her seraphic love for God, with which she blazed beneath the Cross. From the last furrow the Thrones gather her ears worthy of praise and honour in the first Church: her diligent cares and concerns for all.
Having gathered all this together and carried it to one place, they quickly bound a wondrous sheaf and joyfully made ready to deliver it to the heavenly barns.

sections.heading: Christ comes for his Mother

pairs.en: And now came the happy hour of the Virgin's dormition! The Master of the whole world himself, Christ God, rises from his Throne most high, wishing to see the harvest that is at hand. With him rose all who stand before him: the twenty-four elders [see Revelation 4:4] rose from their seats and made ready to go with their King and God. All heaven rose too, so that scarcely anyone remains in it. All of them, in choirs and in regiments, come down from the wide-open furrows of heaven, fill the space of the air, and draw near to the house of the Theotokos.

So God the Son comes to his Mother, the Theotokos, and converses with her with his own most sweet lips. As Meletius, bishop of Sardis, relates, the Lord says to her: “Come, my near one.” And she fell down and worshipped her Lord God with much thanksgiving. With love the Son receives his Most Pure Mother and gladdens her with gracious words. Oh, with what joy in that hour did the Most Pure Virgin repeat her song of old: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced,” and the rest! And with these words she gave up her most pure soul, with great joy, into the hands of her Son and God.

sections.heading: Harvest-home: crowns for everyone

pairs.en: Now the harvest-time is at its end. Already the merry harvest-home is taking shape, and no small number of wreaths are being woven from those same ears of grain. From these crowns of the Most Pure Virgin grace pours out upon everyone; she crowns everyone, for through her all are saved: “And he shall save the world through the Theotokos,” as the Church sings.

From the ear “the Wise Virgin” a crown is woven for all who keep virginity, who have vowed to preserve their purity. From the ear “the Ewe-Lamb of Christ” a crown is woven for the guileless, the meek and the humble. From the ear “the Handmaid of the Lord” a crown is woven for all servants of the Lord who serve God faithfully and with understanding. From the ear “the Fountain of Life” a crown is woven for all who draw streams of water from their eyes and weep at the remembrance of Christ's sufferings, or in sorrow over their own sins. From the most honoured ear “the Crown of the Apostles” a crown is woven for all who hold authority — for Tsars and hierarchs. “Rejoice, honoured crown of pious Kings! Rejoice, honoured boast of reverent priests!” [Akathist to the Most Holy Theotokos]

But those ears themselves, gathered into a sheaf at the Theotokos's death, are also crowned with glory and honour, according to the apostle's words: *“Glory and honour and peace to everyone who does good.”* [Romans 2:10]

The holy apostles take their stand around the Theotokos's deathbed — this is a crown, as it is written: *“Round about him, a crown of brethren.”* [Sirach 50:14] The choirs of the bodiless intelligences encircle her: “The Thrones and Virtues bore her up” [kontakion 12]. The Principalities and Powers surrounded her — and this is a Crown. Christ himself is above her, like a crown above the head. And here was fulfilled what the prophet Isaiah foretold: *“In that day the Lord of Sabaoth will be a crown of hope, woven of glory.”* [Isaiah 28:5] And the most pure soul of the Most Holy Virgin is in the hands of the Lord like the finest of wreaths, as it is written: *“You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.”* [Isaiah 62:3]

sections.heading: The sheaf that stands upright

pairs.en: With such a harvest-home is the wheat of God, the Most Pure Virgin, escorted into the heavenly barns *“with the voice of rejoicing and thanksgiving, with the sound of those who keep festival”* [Psalm 41:5], and presented before the Throne of the Trinity, where God the Father says, in the words of holy Isaac: *“Behold, the fragrance of my Daughter is like the smell of fields filled with wheat.”* [Genesis 27:27] And so God, One in Trinity, gathered his wheat into his barn.

Joseph of the Old Testament once tells his brothers a dream: “We were binding sheaves in the middle of the field, and my sheaf stood upright, while your sheaves stood round about and bowed down to my sheaf.” This was interpreted to mean that Joseph would be a king, and his brothers would have to bow down to him: *“And his brothers said to him: Shall you indeed reign over us, and shall you indeed have dominion over us?”* [Genesis 37:7–8] And so, indeed, it later came to pass.

Not the same, but something incomparably higher, has happened with the most worthy sheaf of the Theotokos's good deeds. The sheaf stood upright; it has been set in a place of honour, at the right hand of the Throne of God: *“The Queen stood at your right hand”* [Psalm 44:10] — in a high place, for truly you are higher than all, O Pure Virgin. Reigning, she reigns over all; ruling, she rules over all. Heaven and earth obey and serve her; and whoever desires and strives to be Christ's wheat, let him gather all his devout feelings into a sheaf and take his stand before that spiritual sheaf in veneration.

To that sheaf the worthy among the wheat of earth bow down, even those crowned with royal crowns: Tsars fall down before it; hierarchs bow, and priests, the clergy and the laity, rich and poor: *“The rich among the people will entreat your face.”* [Psalm 44:13] And the sheaves of the remaining wheat of the saints also offer that same sheaf their fitting veneration. And the twenty-four elders, laying down before her their crowns, speak to her the very words they speak to her Son: *“Worthy are you, O Lady, to receive glory and honour and power.”* [cf. Revelation 5:12] And all things in heaven and on earth, with one voice and with lowest prostration, confess: “It is truly meet to bless you, the Theotokos.”

sections.heading: Our bow and our prayer

pairs.en: Let all of us too render you the veneration that is your due, O Wheat of the bread of life, higher than heaven; and like sheaves on the road and in the open squares, we bow with bodies stretched out flat at your most pure and most holy feet. Our sheaves bow down to your sheaf. And bowing, we lift up our sinful entreaties, hoping to receive from your abundance some small grains of the wheat of your grace.

Wise Virgin — make us wise! Ewe-Lamb of Christ — teach us guilelessness, meekness and humility, and grant that we may be sheep at Christ's right hand! Handmaid of the Lord — rouse us to unwearying service of God! Fountain of life — give us life with the life-giving waters of your grace! Crown of the Apostles — crown with mercy and bounties us who joyfully perform the harvest rites, the harvest-home of your spiritual harvest-field! O Wheat higher than heaven — feed us with bread both of soul and of body all the days of our life! And when the harvest of death comes for our passing life, in which there are more tares than wheat, do you, Most Blessed one, who once entreated your Son to turn water into wine [see John 2:1–9], by those same prayers turn our tares also into wheat; and reap it yourself, gather it yourself, and yourself escort us into the heavenly barns — so that there, no longer from afar as now, but close at hand, face to face, we may render to your Son and our God, the Bread of life, and in God to you also, Most Pure Theotokos, spiritual Wheat, worship, honour, glory and thanksgiving, with all the saints, unto the ages. Amen.
